faqs.a: You need both, and mixing them up is the classic Greek SEO mistake. Local services in Athens or Thessaloniki are searched in Greek script: plumbers, dentists, lawyers, accountants. Tourism, hospitality and anything in the islands is searched in English, by visitors planning from abroad. Many businesses need a Greek section for locals and an English section for tourists, cleanly separated so each ranks for its own queries. I map your revenue to the right language per page, because a hotel that only has Greek pages is invisible to the people booking rooms.
faqs.q: Should my Greek website be in Greek or English?

faqs.a: For tourism businesses, absolutely. TripAdvisor reviews decide bookings on the islands, Google reviews decide local services in the cities, and Greek customers read both carefully. The Hellenic market is small enough that a handful of detailed reviews genuinely move a business, and Greek reviewers write at length when they care. I set up review collection in Greek and English depending on the audience, with owner replies in the reviewer's language, because in Greece the business with the most credible reviews usually gets the booking.
faqs.q: How important are reviews for Greek businesses?

faqs.a: As a citation, yes. xo.gr is the digital heir of the Greek yellow pages, and vrisko.gr describes itself as the number one local-advertising site for Greek small businesses. Google reads both when verifying that your business exists, and older Greek customers still use them directly. Claim and correct both, keep the details identical, then focus your energy on Google Business Profile and TripAdvisor, which is where the customers actually decide. The directories are supporting actors, not the stage.
faqs.q: Are xo.gr and vrisko.gr still worth listing on?

faqs.a: It depends on the season, and Greek SEO has to plan around it. Hotels, restaurants, car rentals and activities on the islands live on a May-to-October cycle, and the smart operators build content and reviews in winter for summer demand. Athens city businesses are steadier year-round, and B2B barely notices the seasons. The mistake is running the same campaign in January and July. I build Greek strategies on the seasonal calendar: content and link-building in the quiet months, review generation and conversion work when the visitors arrive.
faqs.q: Does Greek SEO need to account for the tourist season?

faqs.a: Yes, and it is strict about it. Greek cookie banners must offer a genuine choice, and the Hellenic DPA is active: its 2024 report listed 46 decisions and 4.3 million euros in fines, including 400,000 euros against the Ministry of Interior in a voter-data case. Most Greek small-business sites run banners that do not actually block tracking, which means non-compliant and unreliable data. I fix the banner and the tag setup together, so your analytics are both legal and accurate.

h1: SEO Expert in Greece for Tourism and Local Businesses That Want Bookings
intro:
Greece is a two-speed search market, and SEO here fails whenever someone treats it as one. About 10.3 million people live in the country, with roughly 3.7 million in the Athens metropolitan area and another million around Thessaloniki. But the real number shaping Greek SEO is 43 million: the international visitors who arrived in 2025, the year tourism contributed 32.4 billion euros to the economy. Local services are searched in Greek script by residents; hotels, restaurants, tours and island businesses are searched in English by visitors planning from abroad. One website, two audiences, two keyword universes. Getting this split right is the single most important decision in Greek SEO.

The business hubs each play a different role. Athens concentrates headquarters, services and the largest local search market, with Piraeus next door running one of the Mediterranean's biggest ports and the cruise industry that feeds island tourism. Thessaloniki is the northern commercial center. Heraklion and the rest of Crete, Rhodes, Corfu and the Cyclades are tourism economies where English-language search decides the season. Shipping clusters around Piraeus, agriculture from olive oil to feta across the regions, and a growing startup scene in Athens. Each sector searches differently, and a strategy built only for Athens misses the islands, while a strategy built only for tourists misses the year-round local economy.

Greek is the language of local search, and the Greek alphabet makes keyword research genuinely special. Compounds, transliterations and the mix of Greek and Latin script in queries mean the keyword lists have to be built by someone who understands both. English is the language of tourism search. Many businesses need both languages on the same site, cleanly separated, and the structure matters: Greek pages for Greek queries, English pages for English queries, no mixed-language mush that ranks for neither.

Business culture in Greece is relationship-based. Family ownership is the norm, personal trust outweighs advertising claims, and word of mouth carries weight that no banner ad can buy. That shapes SEO directly: reviews are decisive, the owner's voice matters, and content that feels personal outperforms corporate polish. The regulatory layer is real too: the Hellenic DPA's 2024 report listed 46 decisions and 4.3 million euros in fines, so cookie consent has to be genuine, not decorative. My SEO work in Greece starts from these facts. Greek and English keyword strategy built for the right audience, citations on vrisko.gr and xo.gr, review systems that earn trust in a trust-based culture, and seasonal planning that builds in winter for the summer that pays the bills.

section1.body:
Greece's citation landscape has two domestic pillars and the usual global platforms. vrisko.gr describes itself, in its own stock-exchange company profile, as the number one website for local advertisement of small businesses and professionals in Greece, and Google treats it as exactly that: a core citation source for Greek businesses. xo.gr is the digital descendant of Chrysos Odigos, the Greek yellow pages, and carries the same legacy authority that old directory brands have everywhere. xe.gr, the classifieds giant, rounds out the domestic set. A Greek citation footprint that skips these local sources looks thin to Google, whatever the international aggregators say.

My audits start with NAP consistency done the Greek way. Business names appear in Greek script, sometimes with a Latin transliteration alongside, and both versions need to be consistent everywhere they appear. Addresses follow Greek conventions, and the transliterated versions on international platforms must match: when a street name is spelled three different ways across the web, Google hesitates. I check vrisko.gr, xo.gr, xe.gr and the aggregators for every variation, merge duplicates, close dead listings and make sure island businesses with seasonal addresses do not confuse the data with two locations that are really one.

Tourism businesses need a second citation layer on top of the local one. TripAdvisor is effectively a directory for Greek hospitality: the listing is a citation, a review platform and a booking channel in one, and it has to be claimed, correct and consistent with everything else. Google Business Profile, Booking.com and the sector platforms each carry business data that Google cross-references. I map the platforms that matter for your trade and bring them all into alignment. Then we maintain the footprint through the Greek seasonal cycle: summer hours versus winter hours, seasonal closures, new locations, every change pushed consistently everywhere. In a relationship-based business culture, inconsistent listings do not just weaken rankings. They make the business look unreliable to customers who choose based on trust, and in Greece that costs the booking.

section2.body:
The Google Business Profile is the front door of Greek local search, and for tourism businesses it is the front door, the brochure and the booking desk combined. It sits above the organic results with your reviews, hours, photos and a call or booking button, and for searches like hotel in Santorini or restaurant in Thessaloniki it is where the decision happens. Greek reviewers write at length when they care, which makes a well-reviewed profile enormously persuasive. An unclaimed or review-poor profile does not just lose the ranking. It loses the comparison that follows, in a market where comparisons are everything.

I rebuild Greek profiles for their two audiences. The business description in Greek for local queries and in English where tourists search, each natural and complete rather than translated. Categories chosen for the terms with real search volume in the right language. Photos are decisive: real images of rooms, dishes, premises and views, because tourism customers book with their eyes and local customers trust what they can see. Hours must reflect the Greek seasonal reality: summer hours versus winter hours posted accurately, seasonal closures announced in advance, holiday schedules current. Nothing damages a tourism business like a visitor arriving at a closed door the profile said was open.

Reviews are the core of the Greek profile. I install a review process that asks in the right language at the right moment, Greek for locals, English for visitors, with a direct link that removes friction, and I prepare reply templates so every review gets a genuine owner response in the reviewer's language. In Greece's trust-based culture, the owner's voice in the replies matters as much as the reviews themselves: it shows the personal care Greek customers expect. Then we keep the profile alive year-round: posts about the season, events and offers, questions answered promptly, services current. Google rewards maintained profiles, and in Greece, where trust decides, a living profile with an active owner behind it is the most persuasive marketing asset a local business can own. It works in two languages, around the clock, through every season.

why.heading: Why Greece Needs Its Own SEO Playbook
why.body:
Greece needs specialized SEO because the two-audience split breaks every generic playbook. The first break is language, and it runs deeper than translation. Local searches happen in Greek script, tourism searches in English, and the two keyword universes barely overlap. A hotel needs English pages that rank for hotel in Mykonos and Greek pages that rank for its restaurant among locals. A plumber in Athens needs Greek only. An English-only site is invisible to local customers; a Greek-only site is invisible to the tourists who fill the hotels. I have seen Greek businesses run one-language SEO for years and wonder why half their market never calls. The answer is always the missing language.

The second break is seasonality. Greek tourism businesses live on a May-to-October cycle, and SEO that ignores the calendar wastes the quiet months and panics in the busy ones. Content and link-building belong in winter, when there is time to build; review generation and conversion optimization belong in summer, when the visitors arrive. Athens B2B and year-round local services barely notice the seasons, which means the strategy has to differ by sector, not just by city. Generic SEO runs the same campaign twelve months a year. Specialized Greek SEO runs on the seasonal clock that the revenue follows.

The third break is culture and regulation. Greek business is relationship-based: family ownership, personal trust, word of mouth. SEO content that feels corporate and distant underperforms content with a human voice, and review responses from the owner carry real weight. On the regulatory side, the Hellenic DPA is active, with 46 decisions and 4.3 million euros in fines in 2024, so cookie consent has to be genuine. My approach treats these as ranking factors, because in Greece they are: trust signals convert, and compliance is the foundation of trust. Generic SEO treats Greece as a small market with nice beaches. Specialized SEO treats it as what it is: a two-language, seasonal, trust-driven market where the businesses that win are the ones that feel Greek to Greeks and welcoming to the world.
